opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the impact is big, but maybe not in the way people first imagine.

The most obvious change is on the engineering side. A lot of research is actually engineering: writing experiment code, debugging, plotting, setting up infrastructure, reading through a messy codebase someone else wrote. Models are now really good at this. Things that used to take me an afternoon, like writing a data processing pipeline or figuring out why a training run is behaving strangely, can sometimes take twenty minutes. So the iteration speed of experiments has gone up a lot, and in empirical research, iteration speed is almost everything.

The second change is in reading and learning. When I enter a new area, I used to spend days going through papers just to understand the basic vocabulary. Now I can ask a model to explain the landscape, then go read the key papers myself with much better context. It doesn't replace reading, but it lowers the cost of getting started, so I'm more willing to explore directions outside my comfort zone.

But I'd add a caveat. The part of research that matters most is deciding what problem to work on and what question is actually worth asking. I don't think models have changed that very much yet, at least for me. They can brainstorm and give you ten ideas, but judging which one is important, which one is a dead end, which one has the right timing, that still comes from your own taste and experience. If anything, because execution got cheaper, taste became relatively more important. When everyone can run experiments fast, the bottleneck shifts to asking the right question.

There's also a subtle risk. When the model writes code for you, it's easy to stop understanding the details, and in research the details are often where the surprises are. So I try to stay disciplined: let the model speed things up, but make sure I still understand what's going on, especially when a result looks too good.

So if I put a number on it, maybe I'm several times faster on execution, but the overall research output doesn't scale linearly with that, because the hardest part, figuring out what's true and what matters, is still mostly on us. Though I suspect that will change too, maybe sooner than people expect.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the impact has been enormous, but maybe not in the way people usually imagine. When people ask this question, they often picture a model writing your paper for you or producing some brilliant idea. That's not really what happened to me. The biggest change is that the cost of trying things has collapsed.

As a researcher, a lot of what I used to do was not thinking at all. It was writing boilerplate, setting up environments, debugging some data loader, writing evaluation scripts, converting formats. That stuff probably took half of my time, maybe more. Now I can describe what I want and a model will give me something that works, or at least gets me 80 percent of the way there. So the bottleneck has moved. It used to be execution. Now it's much more about asking the right question and knowing what to try.

That sounds great, and it mostly is, but it also changes what matters in research. If everyone can run ten experiments in the time it used to take to run one, then the differentiator is taste. Which experiments are worth running? What result would actually change how you think? The model doesn't give you that. Sometimes it makes it worse, because it's very easy to generate a lot of activity that feels productive but doesn't go anywhere.

The other thing I'd say is that I use models a lot for thinking, not just coding. Not to get answers, but as something to argue with. I'll write down a half-formed idea and ask it to push back, or to tell me what the obvious objection is. It's often a bit too agreeable, so you have to be careful, but it's still useful to externalize your thoughts and see them reflected back quickly.

So if I had to put a number on it, I'd say I'm maybe two or three times more productive in terms of raw output. But the more honest answer is that the nature of the work changed. I spend less time being a programmer and more time being someone who decides what's worth doing. And I think for the field as a whole, that's the real shift. The scarce thing is no longer the ability to build. It's judgment about what to build.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate productivity into two parts: how quickly I can do something, and whether I’m doing the right thing. AI models help quite a lot with the first part—writing code, working through an idea, or getting a first draft that I can react to. They reduce the cost of trying things, which is valuable for research because many experiments won’t work.

The second part is harder. Choosing a research question, recognizing which result is meaningful, deciding what to pursue—those are still things I need to think carefully about myself. Producing more code or running more experiments doesn’t necessarily mean making more progress.

So I think the biggest benefit is a shorter feedback loop. I can go from an idea to something concrete more quickly, and then use what I learn to decide the next step. But I wouldn’t translate that directly into a claim that I’m some number of times more productive as a researcher.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate productivity into two parts: doing things faster, and deciding what’s worth doing. AI models help a lot with the first part—writing code, debugging, or making a rough idea concrete enough to test. They reduce the cost of trying something, so you can explore more possibilities.

The second part is harder. In research, the bottleneck is often choosing the right question or understanding what an experimental result actually tells you. A model can give you a very plausible explanation, but you still have to judge whether it’s correct and whether it matters.

So I don’t think of the benefit as simply, “I’m twice as productive.” It changes my workflow. I can move faster from an idea to an experiment, but that makes judgment even more important: which experiments should I run, and when should I stop and rethink the premise?
